title: Laude Institute Ships 14 Open Source AI Projects in Slingshots Four
summary:
Various AI tools for agent systems and research decision-making are now available through a collaboration of technical universities. The Laude Institute's Slingshots // FOUR program released 14 projects featuring open source artifacts such as 'maximally-open' models and training data. These projects span multiple layers of the AI stack, from the Thunderkittens kernel to agency frameworks like Headlong and Exo, which support persistent agency and self-improvement through context management.

The release also includes a literature retrieval benchmark called ScholarCatalyst and a reinforcement learning training method named Pedagogical RL. Participating institutions include Stanford, MIT, Carnegie Mellon, and UC Berkeley. Braden Hancock of the institute has opened applications for the fifth batch of research projects.

selectedTweets.text:
Slingshots // Four is live!

Another batch, another fourteen projects shipping open source artifacts that I’m excited about. See below for the full list. A few themes from the batch:

1. Harness time: This quarter harnesses shot up in visibility, with increased appreciation for the parts of an agent that aren’t the model and what they can give you. This batch includes a harness supporting persistent agency (Headlong); a harness supporting self-improvement via context management (ACE); a harness supporting self-improvement of the agentic harness itself (Exo); and a harness supporting multi-agent setups (dotagents).

2. Up and down the stack: There’s innovation to be had at every layer of the stack. We saw projects worth backing at the level of kernels (Thunderkittens); inference (M*); training (Marin); data (Atlantic-CC); evals (Decision Assistants); optimization (SkyDiscover); applications (Wagglehaus), etc.

3. Talk of the town: Slingshots continue to tackle timely problems at the frontier. Concurrent with Jev taking over X, an even faster type 1 decision model (CLM) came out of academia. With RSI on the brain of every big lab researcher, we now have a public literature retrieval benchmark grounded in authors’ firsthand accounts of their research process (ScholarCatalyst). And a new RL training method (Pedagogical RL) addresses head-on the question vexing RL practitioners of how privileged information can be used to discover generalizable behaviors, not just verify.

Congrats to all the researchers in this batch and the previous three who continue to ship their research out into the world with open artifacts that can be adopted and built upon. Open science leads to better outcomes for everyone.

And the good times will continue to roll – batch five is looking just as good. If you’re a researcher with a project that’s gaining momentum and ready for an adrenaline shot, shoot me a DM or apply at https://t.co/HRUiLPRZzT.
